paragraphs: By the time the spring winds of the twenty-first year of Jianyuan reached Guanzhong, Liang Cheng had been home for more than a month.

He had injured his shoulder on the north bank of the Fei River and could scarcely swing a hoe since his return. His wife dragged into the yard a waterwheel that had stood broken for half a year. Beneath the eaves he sat shaving an elm-wood spoke, while his son steadied the timber. The shavings settled on the boy’s shoes like a dusting of snow.

Early one morning the village headman arrived with a paper. The county, he said, had land to allot. Liang Cheng slipped the half-shaped wooden peg into his sleeve and asked first, “Land belonging to my family?”
“Public land. The officials have found it and promised shares to soldiers discharged from the camps and laborers sent home. You’re entitled to a share.”
“Where is it?”

The headman glanced at the irrigation ditch outside Liang’s gate. On the river flats, thirty li away, he said. There had been a flood the year before. No one knew whether a crop could be sown this year.

Liang Cheng felt no joy at the news. He had endured a hundred and eighty-seven days on the military road before he finally came home with a wooden voucher bearing his name and the length of his service. Now the county offered him another piece of writing: it stated how much land he would receive but gave no hint of what the land was like. When his wife heard it was on the river flats, her hand stopped on the winnowing basket. “That ground has flooded twice in three years.”
“I’ll go and look first,” Liang Cheng said.

He took a packet of millet seed from behind the stove, then felt once more for his army voucher. His son asked why they had to seek land when the court had already given them grain and money. Liang passed him the wooden token and told him to read the writing aloud. The boy stumbled through the characters and laughed when he reached “injured right shoulder.” Liang laughed too. Then he took back the token and tucked it against his chest.
“Grain and money run out once you’ve eaten them,” he said. “If the ground grows grain, next year we won’t have to beg anyone.”

That same day, discharged soldiers from several commanderies filled the space outside the Jingzhao prefectural office. They had shed their old armor, but the sword scars across their shoulders and backs remained. Some brought deeds, others military merit tablets. A soldier from Fengyi, with half his left ear missing, held a cracked earthenware bowl in both hands. It contained nothing but damp soil.
When the Prefect of Jingzhao came outside to hear them, he first asked the man why he had brought the earth.
“It’s what I have left of home,” the man said.

His father had left him forty mu of farmland. When he marched away, his child was scarcely a month old, and his wife borrowed twelve shi of millet from the Xue family’s estate. He knew how to recognize his own name, but not the clauses by which property was sold and pledged. He pressed his mark onto the agreement. Only after coming home did he discover that the redemption period had long expired. The wheat was green again, and men hired by the Xue family were cultivating it. The estate owner said the deed was valid, though he would let the veteran stay on as a tenant.
The prefect held the faded deed against the light. “Is this your mark?”
“Yes.”
“No one on the estate forced your hand?”
“No.”
“Then this will be difficult.”

The half-eared soldier set down his bowl and slowly knelt. Everyone thought he was about to cry out for justice. Instead, he merely smoothed the soil in the bowl, as though tidying the ridge of a field too small to plant.

“I went south on the government’s orders. When the government wanted grain, I never withheld what I owed. When it wanted a man, I went. Now I come to the government for a little land, and it tells me to recognize my own thumbprint.”

The prefect did not have him driven away. He ordered a clerk to take the deed inside for inspection. The soldier remained on the steps until the afternoon sun baked cracks through the damp earth in his bowl.
Word of the incident reached the Secretariat just as the land registers of Hedong Commandery arrived.

Heavy curtains left from the winter still hung in the hall, but fresh plans for spring planting covered the desks. The old registers of Anyi recorded 420,000 mu of farmland; judging from grain deliveries in recent years, the Revenue Office reckoned far more land was being cultivated. Some of the unrecorded ground had no claimant because households had fled. Some had been reclaimed along riverbanks, and some lay concealed behind the high walls of fortified estates. The documents carried in by the secretaries had been handled so often that their edges were frayed.
“If there is land, why not distribute it?” Fu Jian asked.

“Your Majesty,” said the Minister of Revenue, pinning one corner of the map with a bamboo slip, “on some land a mu yields a proper harvest; on other land the ground is white with alkali. The registers call both a mu. If we allot the first kind, we must deal with those who farm it now.”

Fu Pi pointed to several fortified estates in Hedong. “When the government withdrew from the disorder, these families opened their granaries, sheltered refugees, and defended their villages. If we measure their fields now and suddenly award to outsiders land they have worked for ten years, the army will have to stay and protect the new tenants from knives.”
Fu Hong looked at his elder brother. “If they cleared it, all the more reason to record it properly. But other fields had owners whose names vanished during the wars.”
“And how do we tell one sort from the other?”
“Look at the old deeds, question the cultivators, and find out when each irrigation channel was built.”
“By the time you’ve finished, spring sowing will be over.” Fu Pi closed the register, his voice cool. “Will you answer to those who have nothing left to put in the pot?”
“Then release grain rations for the landless military households first.”

Fu Pi argued no further. Years of provincial command had taught him how the powerful families of the northern frontier forced men to change their testimony outside a county gate, and what became of those who would not bow along the roads between villages. He feared his younger brother had yet to learn it. Yet Fu Hong faced a hardship of his own: men who had served for years were finding, once their old units were disbanded, that they no longer knew even whom to petition about the wheat fields their families had lost.
Fu Jian listened and tapped the map lightly with a finger.

“Measure first. Where fields are being worked, no one is to pull up boundary posts and change the owner on a single person’s word. Anyone who cannot wait for an allotment is to receive seed grain on loan from the state granaries. And when a fraudulent deed is uncovered, no one is to use the occasion to rob an innocent tenant of his livelihood.”
It was a slow method. Even as the court dispersed, men could be seen shaking their heads.
In the third month, Gao Yunde, a clerk from the Revenue Office of the Secretariat, arrived in Anyi.

Gao was a native of Hedong. In his youth he had copied land-tax accounts in the commandery office. Sent home on this assignment, he brought twenty clerks, forty soldiers, and a dozen or so old farmers who knew the boundaries intimately. He had little taste for official speeches. His first instruction was for the clerks to pull the hemp rope taut, drive in a post at every measured length, then record on the map who tilled the ground, who took the harvest, and who paid the grain tax. Seeing him step through the mud into the fields, the villagers were at first willing to come forward and speak.
On the third day, they confused one Li Shou with another.

Two households bore the same name. One had disappeared years before; the other had lived beside the Mulberry Canal for generations. A correction on an old county sheet was half obscured by fresh ink, and a clerk classified the living family’s fields as abandoned property. Two veterans awaiting land came with official warrants to claim it. The elderly Li sat beneath his mulberry tree with a staff and refused to let them uproot it. The county officers advised him to surrender the ground first and lodge a complaint later.

The north wind was bitter that night. When the party returned next morning, the old man was still propped against the tree, his cuff resting on moss, his body stiff. A physician said he had long suffered from shortness of breath and that the cold dew might have brought back the illness. No one dared say the boundary post had killed him.

Gao Yunde located the original correction in a mildewed village register and ordered the post removed. The two veterans stepped away with their heads lowered. One clutched his millet seed and asked where he was to sow it that year. Gao had no answer.

Li’s son laid the wooden post before his father’s bier. When Gao came to offer condolences, the son would not lift the funeral curtain. He spoke from inside. “You officials can change the field back. Can you change my father back?”

Gao entered the number of the post in the case record. Thereafter, wherever mapped boundaries disagreed with old deeds or actual cultivation, his men measured but did not transfer possession. The clerks grumbled that the assignment would drag on into autumn. “The people driven off their land,” Gao replied, “have more than a single day’s waiting before them.”
It was then that the Cui family’s fortified estate east of Anyi shut its gates against the survey party.

Its walls were high and thick, and rain had blackened the wicker shields on the watchtowers. The steward laid out a feast before the gate. His master was ill, he explained; the visitors could drink first and return to measure the fields in two days. Gao declined. The steward then brought out several dozen tenant farmers and made them kneel together in the wheat.
“Please don’t measure our fields, sir,” said the oldest tenant.
“Are you afraid the survey will show the land isn’t yours?”
“I’m afraid it will show that it is.”
Gao stared at him.

The old tenant’s palms were split with cracks, but his gaze did not waver. “Give me the fields, and next year I may have no seed, the year after no grain. When bandits come down from the western hills, who will guard the estate gate? The state granary is forty li away. When a child runs a fever, who lends us money for a physician? The government may give me land. Can it give me a fortress?”

A short distance away a younger tenant stole a glance at the steward. The moment the steward glared at him, he fell silent. Gao noticed. He understood then that some of these men truly depended on the Cui family, while others hated that dependence and dared not say so.

“Today we record how much land there is; we do not hand it over,” Gao said. “If you owe old debts, we’ll record the debts. Whoever has been cultivating the fields will be recorded as their cultivator. The government’s posts will not turn you out tonight.”
The steward laughed coldly. “Not tonight. What about tomorrow night?”

Gao ordered the ropes laid out. Before the first post could be driven in, a woman rushed forward and wrenched it free. Her son was an archer employed by the estate and stood on the wall. Seeing his mother tangled with the soldiers, he almost loosed an arrow. Gao shouted for a halt, ordered the soldiers to release her, and told the steward to have the bows taken down from the tower. The steward refused. They stood opposed until dark. The survey party retired to the county town without storming the estate.
The next day an unsigned note arrived at the county office: Stop the survey at the Cui estate, and both sides will be left in peace.

The magistrate urged Gao to rest for a few days. He said the Cui family had provided famine relief and loans of grain, and even the county’s clerks and soldiers had benefited from their monthly rations. He acknowledged, too, that for many years the court had paid little attention to the hidden boundaries of Hedong. Gao studied the note by candlelight and slipped it into the case file.
“Tomorrow I’ll go west of town first, not to the Cui estate.”
“That’s wise.” The magistrate relaxed.
“But I must enter that estate eventually. I’ll question the other families first, so no one can say I singled out the Cuis.”

The next morning Gao rode out with only eight soldiers to verify a different tract of land. That afternoon his chestnut official horse came galloping back alone, blood running from one side of the saddle. At nightfall a crowd gathered before the county office. Someone raised a lamp toward the gate tower and saw Gao Yunde hanging beneath its wooden beam, his wrists bound with the hemp rope used for surveying. A wooden board hung on his chest.
Measure our fields today; seize our homes tomorrow.

The magistrate repeatedly ordered the body taken down, but the runners would reach the foot of the steps and retreat. The Cui estate did not open its gates all night. Some in town said the family had hired assassins; others blamed villagers enraged by the survey; still others said Gao had uncovered secrets belonging to another family altogether. No one could produce evidence. Of the eight soldiers who went with him, only three had escaped back; the fate of the others remained unknown.
When Gao’s body was finally lowered, a rolled sketch of field boundaries was still tucked inside his boot. Blood had soaked the writing. Only the character for “mulberry” could be made out.

Five days later, the Governor of Hedong requested five thousand troops to arrest the entire Cui clan. The petition reached the Secretariat and set the court in an uproar. Those advocating force declared that the murder of an official amounted to rebellion, and that the estate must be breached. Someone had already entered Cui farmland on a list of property to be distributed to military households. Pale-faced, Fu Hong held the list under a lamp and asked:
“Who wrote ‘rebel property of the Cui family’?”
The clerk bowed his head. “A provisional designation from the commandery office.”
“Has the case been tried?”
“No.”
“Who killed Gao Yunde?”
“We are still searching for the perpetrators.”

Fu Hong tore the cover from the register and handed it to a subordinate of the Court of Justice. He ordered censors, criminal investigators, and troops from the central army to proceed together to Anyi: first take custody of the county seal and preserve the documents, then prosecute each person for what the evidence proved. The Cui estate was temporarily forbidden to deploy its archers privately; soldiers, in turn, were forbidden to use the investigation as a pretext for demanding grain from it. After the ministers left, Fu Hong looked at the eight words for a long time without speaking.
Fu Pi lingered behind and advised his brother not to imagine that an edict was a suit of iron armor. Fu Hong said he understood. Yet he still looked very young as he spoke the three words.
“You intend to keep measuring?” Fu Pi asked.
“Yes.”
“Where will you begin?”
Fu Hong took out another roll of land registers and passed it to him. They listed estates belonging to the imperial clan, officials, and honored veterans around the capital.
Fu Pi studied it for a long while. “You’ve found yourself more dangerous enemies.”
“If we question only Hedong, no one will believe we aren’t simply seizing land.”
Fu Pi sighed, rolled up the register, and went into the hall to see their father.

At court the following day, an old general who had once marched west with the Fu clan leaned on his cane and asked Fu Jian whether land awarded by the previous ruler still counted. Three of his sons had died in battle, and he had left a leg buried amid the fighting in Longxi. Everyone could see the empty trouser leg.
Fu Jian helped him to his feet. “It counts. Not a single mu granted by edict will be taken from you.”
The old man asked again, “And if the survey finds more than the grant?”
“What you purchased lawfully is yours. What you cleared lawfully will be registered to you. But land seized from another family cannot become yours merely because you have served with distinction.”

The veteran withdrew with his cane. There was no gratitude in his eyes, only a heavy sadness. Watching him, Fu Jian seemed to see every edict of reward he had issued across the years come back to demand an answer. He summoned an assistant director of the Palace Treasury and asked how much land the imperial estates actually held. The official could quote the old register but could not account for the new wheat fields east of the canal.
“Then begin with the imperial estates,” Fu Jian said.

Late that spring, east of Chang’an, survey ropes stretched past a boundary stele of the Heavenly King’s parkland. Onlookers crowded the canal bank. A censor dug beneath the stone marker and found recent broken bricks packed around it: the marker’s position did not agree with the old map. The imperial estate’s steward fell to his knees. The tenant farmers farther off did not cheer. If the boundary of government land changed, they feared, to whom were they to pay their summer rent?

At the boundary, a surveyor drove in a wooden stake and asked a woman carrying a child whether she remembered the old irrigation channel. She pointed deep into a mulberry grove. “My mother-in-law said the inlet was over there. They blocked it last year, and the water stopped reaching our village.”

The clerk added two lines to the scroll. The first stake brought no applause. Only a few old farmers followed the survey rope, bending from time to time to part the wheat shoots and show him an old ridge.

Liang Cheng stood among them. His shoulder still ached, and he held his homecoming voucher. Yet he recognized the knot in the rope beside the canal. At the Fei River, when they dismantled the floating bridge, someone had used that very knot to count its planks. As he watched the rope pass over the imperial estate’s wheat fields, he thought of the waterwheel at home, waiting for water.
“Will they truly be able to give us land this time?” his son asked.
Liang Cheng looked at the millet seed in the child’s hand. “Ask me when you see the first shoots.”
